title: Christ the King
hookLine: the year's last Sunday, instituted in 1925

cards: Crowns had fallen all over Europe in the First World War, and new movements were promising that the nation, or the party, or the leader, deserved everything.
Into that, in December 1925, Pope Pius XI published a letter announcing a brand-new feast. Its name sounded old-fashioned even then: Christ the King.
Real kings were losing their thrones, and the Church named a king who never sat on one. Today it's the last Sunday of the Church's year, the week before Advent starts again.

teach.b: Pius XI's letter, Quas Primas, argued that many of the world's troubles came from pushing Christ out of public life, and that people needed reminding whose kingdom outlasts all the others.
At first the feast fell on the last Sunday of October.

teach.h: MOVED TO THE YEAR'S LAST SUNDAY.
teach.b: After the Second Vatican Council it moved to the last Sunday of the liturgical year, so the year now ends looking toward the end of all things. But here's the twist the feast is built on. Which king?
Watch where the title lands in the passion.

teach.h: MY KINGDOM IS NOT OF THIS WORLD.
teach.b: Before Pilate, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "My kingdom is not of this world." The soldiers dress him in purple and crown him with thorns as a joke.

And the sign nailed above his head, in three languages, says: "THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS." Rome meant it as mockery, a warning to anyone who claimed a crown. Christians came to read it as the plain truth.
In one year of the cycle, the Gospel for this feast is that exact scene: Jesus on the cross, the sign above him, and a criminal beside him asking, Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.
In another, it's the sheep and the goats: the king who says, whatever you did for the least of these, you did for me.

teach.h: A CROWN OF THORNS, A CROSS.
teach.b: So the crown is thorns, the throne is a cross, and the king is found in the hungry and the prisoner.

teach.h: THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.
teach.b: Catholics call him king, and then look at how he reigns.

how: Catholics celebrate the solemnity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, King of the Universe, on the last Sunday of the liturgical year, the Sunday before Advent; some parishes hold a Eucharistic procession or a holy hour.

practice: Think back over this past week: where did your hours actually go? Work, screens, worry, people, sleep; don't judge it, just look, and ask who or what is in charge of your time.
If you pray, offer next week's hours to Christ; if you don't, pick one hour next week to give to something that matters to you.
